questions.topic: Capacitor voltage one time constant into a charge
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a charging capacitor does not reach the supply voltage instantly
questions.stem: The log records a capacitor charging through a resistor and asks why the capacitor voltage does not reach the supply instantly. Explain the shape of the charging curve.

answer.exemplar: While the capacitor charges, a current flows and the charging current falls steadily, so less and less voltage appears across the capacitor as more appears across the resistor. questions.topic: Power in one branch of a parallel pair
questions.learningObjective: Determine the current in one branch of a parallel pair of resistors
questions.stem: The log shows a sketch of two resistors in parallel across a 9.0 V supply, one of 3.0 ohms and one of 6.0 ohms. What current flows through the 6.0 ohm resistor?

options.text: 4.5 A, because the branch current is the supply voltage times the resistance.
options.misconception: multiplies voltage by resistance to get current

options.text: 1.5 A, because the branch has the full 9.0 V across the 6.0 ohms.
0.75 A, because the supply voltage is shared between the two branches.
options.misconception: shares the supply voltage between parallel branches

options.text: 3.0 A, because the two branch resistances add to 9.0 ohms.
options.misconception: adds the branch resistances of a parallel pair

questions.explanation: A parallel branch sees the whole 9.0 V, so the 6.0 ohm resistor carries 1.5 A. The branch currents add in the supply, and neither a shared voltage nor a summed resistance describes a parallel pair.
questions.hint: Each parallel branch sees the whole supply voltage.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Time for a discharging capacitor to fall to a tenth
questions.learningObjective: Correct a mis-stated time for reaching a tenth of the initial voltage
questions.stem: In the log, Marta writes that a 47 microfarad capacitor discharging through a 680 ohm resistor falls to a tenth of its voltage in 0.032 s. Which correction should be made?

options.text: The entry should read 0.69 s, because the tenth level is reached at the half-life point.
options.misconception: confuses the half-life with the tenth level

options.text: The entry should read 3.2 s, because the tenth level comes ten time constants later.
options.misconception: counts ten whole time constants for the tenth level

options.text: The entry should read 0.074 s, because the time constant must be multiplied by the natural log of ten.
The entry should read 0.0032 s, because the tenth level arrives in a tenth of a time constant.
options.misconception: treats a tenth of the charge as a tenth of the time

questions.explanation: The time constant is R C = 0.032 s, and reaching a tenth of the start takes RC ln(10) = 0.074 s. The half-life point is 0.69 of a time constant, and a tenth of the charge is not a tenth of the time.
questions.hint: The time constant multiplied by ln of ten gives the tenth level.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Power lost inside a cell
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a cell becomes warm when it drives a large current
questions.stem: The log records that a heavy cell drives a strong current and still feels warm. Explain where that warmth comes from and why a cell becomes warm when the current is large.

answer.exemplar: The warmth comes from power lost inside the cell, and that loss is the current squared times the internal resistance, I squared r. Because the loss grows with the square of the current, doubling the current makes the heating four times greater. The chemical reactions inside the cell push the charge through the internal resistance, and that resistance turns the energy into thermal energy, which shows up as a warm casing.

questions.explanation: Internal heating follows I squared r, so a larger current heats the cell much more than proportionally. The chemistry drives charge through the internal resistance, and the energy lost there becomes heat in the casing.
questions.hint: The heat inside a cell rises with the square of the current.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Equivalent capacitance of capacitors in series
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the equivalent capacitance of four identical capacitors in series
questions.stem: In the log, four capacitors of 8.0 microfarads each are connected in series. Find the equivalent capacitance in microfarads.
questions.explanation: For identical capacitors in series the equivalent capacitance is C divided by the number of them, so 8.0/4 = 2.0 microfarad. Adding the four values would describe a parallel group.
questions.hint: Identical capacitors in series give C divided by the count.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Mass carried by a given quantity of charge
questions.learningObjective: Count the carriers in a stated quantity of charge
questions.stem: The log records that 3.2 x 10^-5 C of charge passed through a cable. Taking the electron charge as 1.6 x 10^-19 C, find the number of electrons in units of 10^14.
questions.explanation: The carrier count is the total charge divided by the elementary charge, so 3.2 x 10^-5 over 1.6 x 10^-19 = 2.0 x 10^14 electrons. Multiplying instead of dividing answers a different question.
questions.hint: Divide the charge by the charge on one electron.

questions.subject: PHYSICS_II
questions.topic: Potential difference across part of a series chain
questions.learningObjective: Work out the voltage of one cell and of the middle section of a series chain
questions.stem: In the log, a chain of five identical cells in series gives 13.5 V across the whole chain. First find the voltage of a single cell, then find the potential difference across the middle three cells.

options.text: 13.5 V and 8.1 V, because the chain voltage is the same at every point.
options.misconception: keeps the chain voltage for every section

options.text: 2.7 V and 13.5 V, because the middle cells span the whole chain.
options.misconception: claims three middle cells cover the whole chain

options.text: 2.7 V and 5.4 V, because the middle three cells are two pairs of cells.
options.misconception: miscounts the cells in the chosen section

options.text: 2.7 V and 8.1 V, because the total divides equally among five cells and series voltages add.

questions.explanation: Five identical cells sharing 13.5 V give 2.7 V each, so the middle three in series give 8.1 V. A section never keeps the whole chain voltage, and the middle three are three cells, not two pairs.
questions.hint: Divide the chain voltage by the cell count, then add three cells.
